blocks.text: **The problem.** Given an array of strings `strs`, return the longest string that **every** word starts with. If they share nothing, return the empty string.

blocks.alt: flower, flow and flight written in rows, letters lined up in columns. Columns 0 and 1 hold f and l in every row, coloured green. Column 2 holds o, o and i, which disagree, coloured red. The common prefix is fl.

blocks.text: Some string questions need no clever data structure at all: **walk the input once**, keep a tiny bit of state (where you are, the current run, the sign seen so far), and **build the answer as you go** — with a builder or a write pointer, never with `+=` in a loop. The difficulty is in the details: where to stop, what to skip, which edge cases break the loop.

This pattern covers prefixes, compression, parsing numbers, converting between formats (Roman numerals, Zigzag), adding big numbers digit by digit. The three lessons here go from a two-line idea to a careful parser.
1. Sort, then compare the first and last word
Sort the words. In dictionary order, the first and last words are the **most different** ones, and any prefix they share is shared by every word between them. So only those two need comparing.

blocks.code:
def longest_common_prefix(strs):
    words = sorted(strs)                  # the first and last words differ the most
    first, last = words[0], words[-1]
    i = 0
    while i < len(first) and first[i] == last[i]:
        i += 1
    return first[:i]                      # what they share, everyone shares

blocks.text: **Time O(m · n log n), space O(n)** for n words of length up to m: sorting compares strings, each comparison up to m characters.

Use the first word as a guide and compare **column by column**: check that every word has the same character at position 0, then 1, and so on. Stop at the first column where a word disagrees or has already ended.

blocks.caption: Each column must hold the same letter in every row; the first column that doesn't ends the prefix.

blocks.text: **Time O(S), space O(1)** beyond the answer, where S is the total number of characters. In fact it stops after reading only the shared columns plus one, which is often far less.

blocks.alt: Sort, compare ends: O(m·n log n) time, O(n) space. Column by column: O(S) time, O(1) space.

blocks.text: The column scan is the expected answer: it reads no more than it must and needs no extra memory. The sorting trick is worth mentioning as a neat observation.

items: **One word** — the whole word is the prefix.
**An empty word in the list** — the prefix is empty.
**A word that is a prefix of the others** — `["inter", "internet"]`: the scan must stop when the short word ends, not read past it.
**Nothing in common** — the first column already disagrees: `""`.
**Longest Common Suffix** — the same scan from the end of every word.
**Many queries against the same words** — build a trie (prefix tree) once; the prefix is the path down from the root while every node has exactly one child.
**Longest common prefix of every pair** — sort the words; the answer only ever involves neighbours in sorted order.
